overview: Accenture is one of the world's largest professional services companies, providing strategy, consulting, technology, managed services, and increasingly software to more than 9,000 clients, including roughly three-quarters of the Fortune Global 100 and 500 and every G7 government. The company organizes itself around three geographic reporting segments (Americas, EMEA, Asia Pacific) and five industry groups (Products; Health & Public Service; Financial Services; Communications, Media & Technology; and Resources), generating $74.2 billion in FY2026 revenue (ended August 31, 2026) split roughly evenly between Consulting and Managed Services. Accenture is an Irish-domiciled (plc) company operationally headquartered in the US, competing at the top of the global IT services and consulting industry against Deloitte, IBM Consulting, Capgemini, TCS, Infosys, and Cognizant.

business_model.summary: Accenture earns fees from large, project-based consulting/strategy engagements (50% of FY2026 revenue) and longer-duration, contractual Managed Services/outsourcing arrangements (the other 50%) where it runs technology, business processes, or operations for clients over multi-year terms. Growth is driven by 'new bookings' (contracted future revenue, $84.5B in FY2026), which convert to revenue over subsequent quarters, making bookings trends a leading indicator the market watches closely. The company is mid-pivot toward 'Reinvention Services' built around generative and agentic AI, a stance that is simultaneously a growth driver (record bookings, 141 client deals of $100M+ in Q4 FY2026 alone) and a disruptive threat to the labor-hours billing model underpinning both Consulting and Managed Services -- a tension that drove a ~20% single-day stock decline in June 2026 and then a ~20%+ rally in October 2026 as fears eased.

revenue_streams.name: Managed Services
revenue_streams.trend: growing (+8% USD/+6% LC in FY26), though bookings were volatile intra-year (down ~15% YoY in Q3 FY26 before a record Q4)

revenue_streams.name: Consulting
revenue_streams.trend: growing modestly (+5% USD/+3% LC in FY26), impacted by discretionary spending pressure on smaller, shorter-duration contracts

business_model.customer_type: B2B / Enterprise and government -- large corporates (Fortune Global 100/500) and public-sector/federal agencies; ~317 'Diamond' clients are the largest relationships
business_model.industry_mix: Products 30% ($22.5B), Health & Public Service 20% ($15.2B), Financial Services 19% ($14.0B), Communications/Media/Technology 17% ($12.7B), Resources 13% ($9.9B)

competitive_position.market_position: Global scale leader in IT services/consulting; among the largest professional services firms by revenue alongside Deloitte, ahead of IBM Consulting, Capgemini and TCS on disclosed revenue; positioned in the 'implementation giant' tier below the MBB strategy houses, with ~814,000 employees worldwide as of FY2026 year-end.

moat_factors.description: ~814,000 employees and delivery centers across 52 countries let Accenture staff large, complex, multi-geography transformation programs that smaller rivals cannot match; 93% utilization in FY26 shows efficient deployment of that scale.

Long-tenured, embedded Managed Services contracts (85% of top-200 commercial clients and all G7 governments retained 20+ years) create high switching costs, though this base remains the segment most exposed to AI-driven disintermediation.
Serves ~9,000 clients including three-quarters of the Fortune Global 100/500, lending credibility for large, mission-critical engagements.

18 key ecosystem partners (Microsoft, AWS, Google, Nvidia, OpenAI, SAP, Anthropic, etc.) represented ~65% of FY26 revenue and are growing faster than the company overall, positioning Accenture as the preferred implementation layer -- though this also makes it dependent on others' technology roadmaps.

Nearly 110,000 skilled AI and data practitioners as of FY26 year-end, exceeding its three-year goal to double the AI/data workforce; ~$1B/year invested in learning (46 million training hours in FY26) converts headcount into an AI-era asset, but requires continuous, costly retraining.

A growing portfolio of semi-autonomous acquired businesses (Avanade, Dragos, Ookla, LearnVantage, Accenture Construct, Accenture Edge) now ~6% of revenue, giving Accenture adjacent, higher-growth exposure beyond core consulting.

weaknesses: Business model built on billable-hours labor remains structurally exposed to AI/agentic automation, which can compress the hours and headcount needed for the same client outcomes -- Q3 FY26's 15% YoY drop in Managed Services bookings showed this risk is not purely theoretical
High exposure to discretionary client IT/consulting budgets, which are cut quickly in downturns, policy shifts, or hawkish-rate environments
Limited proprietary/IP-driven recurring revenue relative to software companies; revenue is largely people- and project-based despite a growing software ambition

Thin differentiation versus IBM, Capgemini, TCS, and Big 4 advisory arms on large deals, and increasing competition from AI-native companies and growing in-house GCCs, which can pressure pricing (lower pricing was noted in Q4 FY26)

Federal/public-sector revenue concentration (~7% of total, 14% of Americas, 34% of Health & Public Service) creates political/budget-cycle risk that has already dented Public Service growth in the Americas

growth_drivers: Generative and agentic AI-related 'Reinvention Services' bookings and revenue as clients fund AI transformation programs; a record 141 client bookings of $100M+ in Q4 FY2026 alone and full-year bookings of $84.5B reassured the market that AI is a net demand driver, not purely a headwind

Aggressive, well-funded M&A strategy -- $4.9B across 17 strategic acquisitions in FY2026 (Dragos/runZero/NetRise OT cybersecurity for ~$4.2B, Ookla network intelligence, Faculty AI/decision intelligence, DLB data centers, Alfahealth digital health), with ~$5B of further acquisition spend planned for FY2027 focused on AI, data, and cybersecurity capabilities
Continued cloud migration, data modernization, and cybersecurity demand across enterprise and government clients, reinforced by the new OT/industrial cybersecurity platform from Dragos
Reorganization into 'Reinvention Partners' and 'Reinvention Engines' aimed at cross-selling AI-enabled consulting and managed services across a unified operating model
Expanding 'Network of Businesses' (Avanade, Accenture Construct, Accenture Edge, LearnVantage, Ookla) now ~6% of revenue, providing adjacency growth beyond core consulting/managed services

Continued capital return program -- at least $9.5B targeted for FY2027 (on top of a record $11.5B returned in FY2026), a $6B additional buyback authorization approved September 2026, and a 5% dividend increase to $1.71/share quarterly
AI safety as an emerging growth/differentiation area, with a newly announced commitment to invest at least $1.0 billion over the next five years

business.risk: AI/agentic disruption of the core billable-hours model
business.description: Analysts have repeatedly flagged that agentic AI can compress the labor-intensive work (strategy analysis, implementation, managed services/BPO) underpinning Accenture's revenue base; Managed Services bookings fell ~15% YoY in Q3 FY2026 before rebounding sharply in Q4, showing the risk remains live even after the Q4 reassurance. Accenture also stopped disclosing separate GenAI bookings/revenue figures after Q1 FY2026, reducing investor visibility into the trend.

business.risk: Client concentration in large discretionary transformation deals
business.description: Revenue depends on large enterprise/government clients continuing large-scale, multi-year technology and consulting spend; deal delays (large Managed Services deals pushed from FY26 into FY27) directly hit bookings and create lumpiness.

Competes with Deloitte, IBM Consulting, Capgemini, and lower-cost offshore players (TCS, Infosys, Cognizant, Wipro) on price, and increasingly with AI-native software companies and clients' own growing in-house global capability centers (GCCs) that can substitute for outside consulting.

financial.risk: Margin pressure from pricing and restructuring costs
financial.description: Management noted 'lower pricing in many areas' during Q4 FY2026; the prior six-month business optimization program ($923M combined in FY25-FY26, primarily severance) was completed in Q1 FY2026 but similar actions could recur if demand softens.

A weaker U.S. dollar added ~2 points to FY2026 USD revenue growth versus local currency; management expects FY2027 USD and local-currency growth to be roughly equal assuming rates hold, but a dollar reversal would be a headwind.

financial.risk: Rising debt load to fund M&A
financial.description: Outstanding long-term senior notes reached $10 billion as of FY2026 (maturing 2027-2036) to help fund the accelerated acquisition program; while leverage remains low relative to cash flow, the pace of debt-funded M&A is increasing.

regulatory.description: Federal work (~7% of total FY26 revenue, ~14% of Americas revenue, ~34% of Health & Public Service revenue) continues to be a drag, with Public Service revenue declining in the Americas in FY2026 amid continued government cost-cutting and procurement uncertainty.

Evolving and diverging AI regulation (EU AI Act, GDPR, Digital Operational Resilience Act, Cyber Resilience Act, U.S. state privacy laws) could raise compliance costs, limit certain AI offerings, or slow AI-related sales cycles across jurisdictions.

Increases in the cost of obtaining or maintaining H-1B or similar visas, or requirements to pay higher wages to visa holders, could raise delivery costs and constrain Accenture's ability to deploy talent globally.

macro.risk: Discretionary IT/consulting spend sensitivity to the economic cycle
macro.description: Consulting and large transformation projects are among the first budget items cut in a slowdown; most consulting contracts are terminable on 30 days' notice, and even Managed Services contracts can be delayed or renegotiated.

The 10-K continues to flag the ongoing Middle East conflict and broader geopolitical and trade-policy volatility (tariffs, protectionism) as factors that have adversely affected, and could continue to affect, client demand in certain regions.

execution.description: Headcount grew to ~814,000 in FY2026 (from ~779,000) even as the company continued reskilling toward AI roles (now ~110,000 AI/data practitioners); balancing hiring, attrition (13% voluntary in FY26) and involuntary terminations against shifting AI-era demand remains an ongoing execution challenge, and local works-council requirements in some countries constrain flexibility.

execution.risk: Integration of an accelerated M&A pace
execution.description: FY2026's $4.9B across 17 deals, including the ~$4.2B Dragos/runZero/NetRise OT-cybersecurity combination, plus a further ~$5B planned for FY2027, raises integration risk across a growing number of simultaneous acquisitions in AI, data, and cybersecurity.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: The global IT services/consulting industry experienced its most significant AI-driven repricing event in 2026: a mid-year selloff (Accenture, and by extension peers, fell sharply in June 2026) on fears that agentic AI would structurally compress labor-hours economics, followed by a sharp recovery in October 2026 after Accenture's record bookings quarter eased those fears and lifted IT-services peers (Infosys, IBM, Capgemini) as well. The sector outlook remains bifurcated between near-term AI-transformation spending as a tailwind and longer-term uncertainty over how AI reshapes project economics and headcount needs.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate-to-high -- consulting and discretionary technology spend are among the more cyclical corporate budget items (most consulting contracts are cancellable on 30 days' notice); Managed/outsourcing revenue is comparatively more resilient due to contractual, multi-year terms, though 2026 showed even this base can see sharp, quarter-to-quarter booking swings.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate indirect sensitivity -- higher rates and a hawkish Fed were cited as pressuring IT-services valuations and client capex/opex decisions during the mid-2026 selloff; direct balance-sheet sensitivity is low given Accenture's $12.8B cash position, though the company now carries $10B in long-term debt to help fund M&A.
macro_factors.currency_exposure: Significant -- over half of revenue is generated outside the Americas (EMEA + Asia Pacific = 50% of FY26 revenue), and reported USD growth diverges from local-currency growth (FY26: +6% USD vs +5% LC) depending on dollar strength; major hedged exposures include USD/INR, USD/JPY, USD/GBP, USD/EUR and USD/PHP.
key_input_costs: Skilled labor / compensation costs (68% of revenue is cost of services)
Technology/cloud and AI platform licensing costs passed through to clients
Acquisition integration and R&D spend (~$1.0B R&D in FY26)

recent_developments.event: Q4 and full-year FY2026 earnings beat expectations and eased AI-disruption fears: Q4 revenue of $18.68B (+6% USD/+7% LC, above the $17.75-18.40B guided range), record new bookings of $22.2B in the quarter (book-to-bill 1.2) including a record 141 client bookings of $100M+, and FY2026 revenue of $74.18B (+6%/+5% LC) with FY2026 bookings of $84.5B. Shares surged roughly 20-23% intraday, among the largest single-day gains in company history, and the rally lifted IT-services peers Infosys and IBM as well.

Stock continued rallying after the Q4 print, reportedly up ~74.6% over the three months to October 21, 2026 from its mid-2026 lows; analysts split on the move -- Wells Fargo raised its price target to $252 (from $210) and UBS to $300 (from $278) on October 26, while Baird downgraded the stock to Hold on October 21 on valuation grounds even while nudging its target up to $252.

Board of Directors approved $6.0 billion of additional share repurchase authority (bringing total outstanding authority to ~$6.94B as of the FY2026 10-K) and declared a quarterly dividend of $1.71 per Class A share, a 5% increase, as part of FY2027 guidance for at least $9.5 billion in total shareholder returns.

Accenture closed its largest cybersecurity acquisition to date, taking a majority stake in Dragos along with runZero and NetRise for a combined OT/industrial-cybersecurity platform valued at roughly $4.2 billion, the centerpiece of FY2026's $4.9B spent across 17 strategic acquisitions (also including Ookla, Faculty, DLB, Whalar, Comware and Alfahealth).

Shares fell roughly 18-20% in a single day to a 52-week low after new bookings fell ~2% YoY (Managed Services bookings down ~15% YoY on large-deal push-outs to FY2027) and management cut full-year FY2026 revenue growth guidance to 3-4% local currency (from a 3-5% range set in March); commentary cited both a hawkish rate environment and AI-driven uncertainty over consulting/managed-services demand.

CEO Julie Sweet gave extensive commentary (Fortune) on restructuring Accenture's organizational model around AI, tying promotions to AI fluency and describing the workforce transition as still in its difficult early stages.

Q1 FY2026 revenue of $18.7B (+6% USD/+5% LC) and record new bookings of $20.9B (+12% USD); the company's six-month business optimization program (primarily severance, ~$923M combined with the prior fiscal year) was completed during the quarter.

Accenture reported FY2025 revenue of $69.7B (+7%) and disclosed ~$615M in FY2025 restructuring charges and a workforce reduction of roughly 11,000-12,000 roles tied to AI reskilling, alongside continued hiring of AI/data specialists.

items.notes: First FY2027 guide, issued alongside Q4 FY26 results; the range explicitly includes inorganic contribution from acquisitions. Implied USD revenue of $76.4-$78.7B versus FY2026 actual of $74.2B. Follows FY2026's final actual growth of 5% LC, which beat the mid-year-cut guidance of 3-4%.
Represents continued expansion from FY2026's 15.4% GAAP / 15.8% adjusted operating margin.
Implies roughly 6-9% growth over FY2026's GAAP diluted EPS of $13.56.
Roughly flat to modestly higher versus FY2026 actual free cash flow of $11.62 billion.
Set as a floor; FY2026 actual cash returned to shareholders was $11.5 billion ($7.5B buybacks + $4.0B dividends), so this figure is a minimum rather than a point estimate.

Below the $9 billion acquisition target management floated mid-FY2026 (June 2026) amid the growth scare; actual FY2026 acquisition spend came in at $4.9 billion across 17 deals, and FY2027 guidance of ~$5B signals a similar, still-elevated but more measured pace focused on AI, data, and cybersecurity.
A 5% increase over the prior quarterly rate; additional quarterly dividends expected to be declared in December 2026 and March/June 2027.

guidance.management_commentary: CEO and Chair Julie Sweet characterized FY2026 as 'another year of broad-based growth,' pointing to a record 141 client bookings of $100M+ in Q4 alone as evidence that AI-driven transformation demand is additive to, not simply a replacement for, traditional consulting and managed-services spend. Management continues to frame the AI transition as requiring sustained investment -- citing nearly 110,000 AI/data practitioners (exceeding its three-year goal to double that workforce) and a newly announced plan to invest at least $1.0 billion over five years in AI safety -- while acknowledging that pricing remained competitive and some large deals continued to shift between fiscal years. FY2027 guidance explicitly folds in acquisition-driven growth, reflecting a strategy of buying AI, data, and cybersecurity capability (notably the ~$4.2B Dragos OT-cybersecurity platform) rather than relying solely on organic reinvention of the existing labor-based model.

bull_case: Q4 FY2026's record bookings (141 deals of $100M+, $84.5B in full-year bookings, book-to-bill of 1.2) suggest the market's mid-2026 AI-disruption fears were overstated, with both Consulting and Managed Services reaccelerating

FY2027 guidance for continued margin expansion (15.9-16.1% from 15.4%) and EPS growth (6-9%) alongside only modest revenue growth signals confidence in cost discipline and mix improvement even in a slower-growth environment

Scale, global delivery footprint, and deep ecosystem partnerships (18 partners generating ~65% of FY26 revenue and growing faster than the core business) position Accenture as the default large-scale integration partner for enterprise AI adoption

Disciplined, well-funded capital returns (at least $9.5B targeted for FY2027, a $6B incremental buyback authorization, and a 5% dividend increase) support total shareholder return, and the company is deploying M&A (~$5B FY27) into genuinely higher-growth niches like OT cybersecurity (Dragos) and data/network intelligence (Ookla)
Several sell-side analysts raised price targets meaningfully after the Q4 print (Wells Fargo to $252, UBS to $300), reflecting renewed confidence in the growth/margin trajectory
bear_case: The structural AI/agentic-automation threat to the billable-hours model has not been resolved, only de-risked for one quarter -- Managed Services bookings fell 15% YoY as recently as Q3 FY2026, and Accenture stopped disclosing separate AI bookings/revenue metrics after Q1 FY2026, reducing investor ability to track the trend independently

The stock has already rallied roughly 70%+ off its mid-2026 lows in a matter of months; Baird downgraded to Hold on valuation grounds even while raising its target, and some analysts estimate fair value below the post-rally price, raising the bar for further upside

US federal government spending remains a structural drag (~7% of total revenue, 34% of Health & Public Service revenue), with Public Service revenue in the Americas still declining in FY2026 amid ongoing budget and procurement uncertainty

The accelerated acquisition pace ($4.9B across 17 deals in FY2026, including the ~$4.2B Dragos platform, with ~$5B more planned for FY2027, partly funded by $10B in long-term debt) raises integration and capital-allocation risk at a time when organic growth visibility is still being rebuilt

Intensifying competition from AI-native software vendors and clients' own growing in-house global capability centers (GCCs) could structurally compress consulting margins and demand over the medium term, even if near-term bookings look strong
